title: Andreev-reflection spectroscopy of SrPt3P single crystals
authors: Valeriy A. Stepanov, Nikolai D. Zhigadlo, Erik Piatti, Dario Daghero
abstract: The interplay between inversion symmetry breaking and superconducting pairing mechanisms is a long-standing puzzle of solid-state physics. Ternary platinum phosphide SrPt$_3$P is an excellent case study in this regard, since it shares the distorted anti-perovskite crystal structure of non-centrosymmetric superconductor CePt$_3$Si but preserves the inversion symmetry center, enabling a direct comparison between the two compounds. Despite intense scrutiny, the superconducting pairing strength, gap symmetry, and magnitude of SrPt$_3$P remain an open question. Here, we study the gap structure of high-quality SrPt$_3$P single crystals with $T_c = 8.6$ K by using point-contact Andreev-reflection spectroscopy. The spectra systematically showed symmetric conductance maxima and a zero-bias minimum, as is typical of fully gapped superconductors, and dips at finite voltage $V_\mathrm{dip}$ due to the local transition of the contact region to the resistive state. In contacts with high resistance, where the dips fall sufficiently far from the gap features, the conductance curves can be well fitted with a single isotropic $s$-wave gap. The temperature dependence $Δ(T)$ of the gap amplitude extracted from the fit is in good agreement with the one predicted by the BCS theory, with a zero-temperature mean value $Δ(0)=1.88\pm0.08$ meV, and a mean gap ratio $2Δ/k_\mathrm{B}T_c = 5.2\pm0.2$.
summary: This work uses point-contact Andreev-reflection spectroscopy on $	ext{SrPt}_3	ext{P}$ to investigate its superconducting gap structure. The measurements reveal a fully gapped, isotropic $s$-wave pairing symmetry, yielding a gap value consistent with BCS theory. This result helps resolve ambiguities regarding the pairing mechanism in this material.
main_problem: The study aims to determine the superconducting pairing strength, gap symmetry, and magnitude of $	ext{SrPt}_3	ext{P}$, particularly in the context of inversion symmetry breaking in superconductors.
main_result: The Andreev reflection spectroscopy strongly suggests that $	ext{SrPt}_3	ext{P}$ possesses an isotropic, nodeless $s$-wave superconducting gap, with a BCS-like temperature dependence.
method: Point-contact Andreev-reflection spectroscopy ($	ext{d}I/	ext{d}V$) was performed on high-quality single crystals to probe the superconducting energy gap.
model_or_system: The physical system is the ternary platinum phosphide $	ext{SrPt}_3	ext{P}$, a centrosymmetric superconductor. The analysis utilizes the Blonder, Tinkham, and Klapwijk (BTK) model to fit the conductance spectra.
key_observables: Symmetric conductance maxima, zero-bias minimum, temperature dependence of the gap amplitude $\Delta(T)$, and the gap ratio $2\Delta/k_B T_c$.
important_parameters: Zero-temperature mean gap value $\Delta(0) = 1.88 \pm 0.08 	ext{ meV}$ and a mean gap ratio $2\Delta/k_B T_c = 5.2 \pm 0.2$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of the BTK model and that the observed gap structure is dominated by the intrinsic superconducting properties rather than contact artifacts (like the observed conductance dips).
figures_summary: Figures show magnetization curves confirming $T_c = 8.6 	ext{ K}$, example I-V curves exhibiting excess current, and comparisons of superconducting vs. normal state transport.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the context of pairing symmetry puzzles, details the Andreev spectroscopy measurements on $	ext{SrPt}_3	ext{P}$, analyzes the data using the BTK model, and concludes by comparing the fit results against theoretical predictions for nodal vs. isotropic gap symmetries.
why_interesting: The detailed spectroscopic measurements provide quantitative parameters ($\Delta(0)$, gap ratio) for a specific superconducting material, which is crucial data for comparing against theoretical models of unconventional superconductivity.

FIG. 2. Differential conductances of four “soft” SrPt3P/Ag point contacts (PC1 to PC4) with normal-state resistances RN = 43.5,16.4,13.8 and 2.0Ωat different temperatures. On decreasing the contact resistance, the conductance minima shift towards lower energies, as expected for dips due to the attainment of the critical current in the contact region, partially eroding the signatures of the superconducting gap.

FIG. 3. Differential conductance of PC2, recorded at T = 4.37 K (symbols), normalized to the curve at 8.6 K, together with the relevant best-fitting curves (lines) obtained by an automatic least- square fitting procedure restricted to different energy ranges: ±2.0 meV (red), ±2.5 meV (green) and ±3.0 meV (blue). The inset shows a magnification of the region of the maximum and highlights the extremely good agreement between experiment and calculations up to 2.5 meV, as well as the practical indistinguisha- bility of the three fitting curves in this energy scale.
